content: 1. The study utilized data from January 2002 and was conducted as a retrospective analysis. 2. The research aimed to evaluate the role of disadvantaged socioeconomic status in unintentional injuries among children. It found that even after adjusting for housing quality and the use of safety equipment (such as fireguards, safety gates, smoke alarms, and electric socket covers), children from less advantaged backgrounds still experienced a higher rate of injuries. 3. Interestingly, children living in households without any of the four home safety devices were approximately 20% less likely to sustain injuries compared to those living in homes equipped with all four devices. 4. Only exposure-outcome pairs relevant to the systematic review and with adjusted data were reported. 5. For the fireguard analysis, only households with active heating systems (e.g., gas, wood, coal, or electric fires) were included, as fireguards were deemed irrelevant for other types of homes. 6. The study relied on secondary data, and the outcome assessment was passive, with mothers reporting injury events. However, the exposure assessment was objective, which is a notable strength of the study. 7. A systematic review on home injuries was conducted for the WHO Housing and Health Guidelines. Study: Sadeghi Bazargan (2012) 8. This case-control study in Ardabil Province, Iran, investigated household-related predictors of burn injuries. 9. Cases included patients with unintentional thermal burn injuries (e.g., scalds, flame burns, and contact burns) admitted to the Ardabil Burn Center. 10. Controls were age-, sex-, and urbanity-matched individuals without a history of burn injuries in the month prior to enrollment, admitted to other hospital wards in the same region. 11. Exclusion criteria for cases included frostbites, chemical burns, self-immolation, intentional burns, burns occurring outside Ardabil Province, and outpatient admissions. 12. Controls excluded individuals admitted for chronic diseases, other major injuries, or outpatient admissions. 13. All inpatient burn victims were enrolled, regardless of their outcome (discharge, death, or transfer). 14. The study attempted to identify numerous predictors but did not report the similarity between cases and controls in terms of demographic factors like age and gender. Study: Harvey (2013) 15. This retrospective cohort study in New South Wales, Australia, examined the impact of smoke alarm legislation on residential fire injuries and smoke alarm ownership from 2002 to 2010. 16. The legislation, introduced in 2006, mandated that all homes have at least one smoke alarm. 17. Data on smoke alarm ownership and demographics were obtained from the NSW Population Health Survey. 18. The study identified 437 hospitalizations for residential burns during the study period. 19. A limitation of the study was the potential for confounding factors, such as increased awareness before and after legislative changes, which could not be ruled out. 20. Smoke alarm ownership data were collected via telephone, introducing potential reporting bias. Study: Chamania (2015) 21. This interventional study in rural Madhya Pradesh, India, assessed the feasibility of replacing kerosene lamps with solar-powered and LED lamps to reduce burn injuries. 22. A total of 1,042 households from 18 villages were randomly selected for the intervention. 23. At baseline, villagers reported 23 burn incidents over the past five years. Six months after introducing alternative lighting, only one burn incident (suicidal and unrelated to the lamps) was reported. 24. The study had limitations, including a short follow-up period (6 months) and lack of adjustment for confounders. However, it provided valuable contextual data from a region with limited prior research. Study: Keall (2015) 25. This cluster-randomized controlled trial in New Zealand evaluated home modifications to reduce fall-related injuries. 26. Participants were individuals living in homes that had recently received government-subsidized insulation retrofits. 27. The intervention group (436 households) received home modifications, such as handrails, grab rails, non-slip mats, and improved lighting, along with a home safety pamphlet. The control group (406 households) did not receive these modifications or the pamphlet. 28. The intervention group experienced a 26% reduction in the rate of medically treated falls compared to the control group after adjusting for age, sex, previous falls, and ethnicity. 29. The study was methodologically robust, with proper randomization and allocation. However, the educational value of the pamphlet could not be separated from the effect of the home modifications. Study: Kendrick (2015) 30. This multicenter case-control study in the UK investigated risk and protective factors for falls from furniture in children aged 0–4 years. 31. Cases were children who experienced a fall from furniture and required medical attention, while controls were children without such falls on the same date. 32. Controls were matched to cases by age, sex, calendar time, and general practice. 33. Recruitment involved inviting 10 controls per case via mail, with additional measures like personalized invitations and vouchers to improve participation. 34. The study had a low participation rate but was comparable between cases and controls. Study: Kamei (2015) 35. This randomized controlled trial in Tokyo, Japan, evaluated the effectiveness of a home hazard modification program (HHMP) in reducing falls among older adults (≥65 years). 36. The intervention included education and practice on home safety using a model mock-up of a typical Japanese home. 37. The study found a reduction in overall and indoor fall events among participants. 38. However, it was judged to have a high risk of bias in several domains, including blinding, outcome measures, and selective reporting. Study: Stewart (2016) 39. This multicenter case-control study in England examined modifiable risk factors for scald injuries in children under 5 years. 40. Cases were children with scald injuries requiring medical attention, while controls were children without scald injuries. 41. Controls were frequency-matched to cases by age and sex. 42. Recruitment involved identifying eligible controls from practice registers and inviting them to participate via mail. 43. The study provided insights into safety behaviors, safety equipment, and home hazards related to scald injuries.
